National Credit Union Administration

12 CFR Part 701

RIN 3133-AF93

AGENCY:

National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).

ACTION:

Final rule.

SUMMARY:

The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule to amend its criteria for determining associational common bonds. The amendments clarify that requiring members to buy a good, product, or service from a group as a condition of membership will no longer automatically bar eligibility as a recognized association. After considering public comments, the Board finalizes the proposed rule with certain modifications. The Board's revisions detail how NCUA assesses client-customer relationships (including relevant examples). These changes also simplify NCUA's process for reviewing pre-approved groups.

DATES:

This final rule is effective on January 4, 2027.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

John Tamashiro, Director, Division of Consumer Access, Office of Credit Union Resources and Expansion at (703) 548-2577 or 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314, or Keisha Brooks, Attorney-Advisor, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at the above address.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Introduction

A. Background

The Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act) recognizes three types of federal charters—single common bond (occupational and associational), multiple common bond (more than one group each having a common bond of occupation or association), and community. NCUA's Chartering and Field of Membership Manual, incorporated as Appendix B to part 701 of NCUA's regulations (Chartering Manual) implements the FCU Act.[1]

For chartering purposes, a common bond is a fundamental requirement for a recognized association.[2]

In the Credit Union Membership Access Act (CUMAA), Congress found that “[a] meaningful affinity and bond among members, manifested by a commonality of routine interaction, shared and related work experiences, interests, or activities, or the maintenance of an otherwise well understood sense of cohesion or identity is essential to the fulfillment of the public mission of credit unions.” [3]

While the FCU Act does not explicitly define “common bond,” the Board clarified its meaning in the Chartering Manual. A common bond is the characteristic or combination of characteristics which distinguishes a particular group of persons from the general public.[4]

Furthermore, the Chartering Manual defines an associational common bond to include individuals and groups whose members participate in activities developing common loyalties, mutual benefits, and mutual interests.[5]

Within this framework, the Chartering Manual reflects a long-standing policy that associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship do not meet associational common bond requirements.[6]

Based on agency experience with particular requests, the members of an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship had only an interest in purchasing a good, product, or service from the group.[7]

The group operated in a manner indistinguishable from a vendor providing a good, product, or service to the general public. Its charter and bylaws lacked provisions for membership governance or qualifications beyond paying for a good, product, or service. Membership fees (in terms of amount, timing, and structure) functioned merely as payments for a good, product, or service.

Still, the Chartering Manual does not preclude an association with an incidental client-customer relationship if other associational common bond requirements are met.[8]

In such circumstances, NCUA staff generally considered a client-customer relationship as incidental when it served a secondary role in relation to the group's associational common bond and activities. For this purpose, NCUA often considered multiple factors.

For example, past chartering policies mentioned electric cooperatives as groups that could meet associational standards, even though purchasing

( printed page 73657)

power was required.[9]

These chartering policies noted that an electric cooperative must make a strong showing of common activities. Another important factor was electric cooperatives' distinctive relationship with their members. Unlike other client-customer groups, these members are both the owners and users of the cooperative.

The Chartering Manual also included one example of an incidental client-customer relationship—a fraternal association that offers insurance, which is not a condition of membership. This example led to the conclusion that, if a fraternal benefit association required its members to buy insurance from the group as a condition of membership, the association was automatically disqualified.[10]

On April 8, 2026, the Board announced its proposal to amend the Chartering Manual to clarify that a multifaceted approach remains NCUA's position, even if purchasing a good, product, or service from a group is a condition of membership.[11]

In the proposed rule, the Board preserved the long-standing policy that an association based primarily on a client-customer relationship does not qualify as a recognized association. The Board proposed eliminating the fraternal association example of an incidental client-customer relationship that had been interpreted as automatically barring some groups with a mandatory purchase condition from associational eligibility. As proposed, NCUA would evaluate the circumstances as a whole. The comment period ended on June 8, 2026.

The final rule adopts the April 8, 2026, proposed rule with certain modifications discussed more fully in the section summarizing the comments. After carefully considering the public comments, the Board is amending the April 8, 2026, proposal to increase transparency into NCUA's process for reviewing client-customer relationships. These changes explain key considerations and provide examples. The Board's other changes aim to make NCUA's pre-approved group reviews more efficient. The final rule amends the associational common bond criteria applicable to single associational charters and multiple common bond federal credit unions (FCUs). Accordingly, the final rule does not apply to occupational common bond charters, community charters, or federally insured state-chartered credit unions.

B. Legal Authority

The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).[12]

The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.[13]

Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.[14]

Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.[15]

Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.

The Board is also issuing this final rule pursuant to its rulemaking authority under Section 109 of the FCU Act.[16]

Section 109 of the FCU Act establishes the field of membership framework for FCUs.[17]

Section 109 also describes the membership criteria for federal charters and grants the Board rulemaking authority with respect to such charters.[18]

Section 109(d)(3) further directs the Board to issue guidelines or regulations, after notice and opportunity for comment, setting forth the criteria that the Board will apply in determining whether a group may be added to an FCU's field of membership.[19]

Sections 109(a) and 109(f)(2)(E) reference more general rulemaking authority with respect to associational groups and fields of membership.[20]

Pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act, the Board implements these statutory requirements through the Chartering Manual.

II. Final Rule

A. Overview

This final rule follows publication of the April 8, 2026, proposed rule, and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on June 8, 2026, the Board received 18 public comments. Comments were submitted by credit union trade associations, credit union leagues, FCUs, one associational group, an individual, and a bankers association. All commenters except one supported the proposal. Most commenters supported considering a group's structure, purpose, and activities rather than automatically excluding the group based on a mandatory purchase condition. Several commenters urged NCUA to clarify certain aspects of the proposal, including definitions, examples, and documentation guidelines. One bankers association opposed the proposal.

After carefully considering the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has made the following changes to the proposal: (1) detailing NCUA's criteria in reviewing client-customer relationships, (2) adding relevant examples, and (3) simplifying NCUA's review process for pre-approved groups.

B. Discussion of Public Comments

This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.

Comments on NCUA's Statutory Authority

Several commenters observed that the proposal was consistent with NCUA's statutory authority, noting that neither the FCU Act nor CUMAA requires disqualifying associations due to a client-customer relationship. Most commenters agreed that a mandatory purchase condition should not automatically bar eligibility as a recognized association if the client-customer relationship is incidental to the association's mission and activities. Many commenters observed that the proposal provides measured regulatory relief for single associational and

( printed page 73658)

multiple common bond FCUs. Two commenters described the categorical exclusion based on a mandatory purchase condition as an unnecessarily restrictive barrier to groups with legitimate common bonds. Another commenter highlighted that eliminating the exclusion would provide additional flexibility for small FCUs when adding associations to their fields of membership. Another commenter noted that imposing eligibility restrictions beyond statutory requirements could reduce consumer access to affordable financial services from FCUs. According to this commenter, such barriers diminish competition in local financial services markets and leave consumers with fewer options, particularly those of modest means.

One bankers association opposed the rule, contending that, contrary to congressional intent, the proposal contributed to the erosion of field of membership restrictions under the FCU Act. Citing concerns regarding competitive equity and statutory fidelity, the commenter observed that the distinctive legal and tax status of FCUs is justified by their restricted mission and membership. This commenter noted that the proposed amendment, while narrow in isolation, is part of a series of incremental changes that collectively could greatly expand credit union membership beyond congressional intent.

NCUA Response.
The Board welcomes the comments submitted on its April 8, 2026, proposed rule. After careful consideration, the Board believes that the regulatory changes are within the broad authority conferred in the FCU Act and consistent with congressional intent.

Section 109 of the FCU Act authorizes the Board to establish regulations for determining which groups meet field of membership requirements for FCUs.[21]

Exercising this authority, the Board has periodically amended the Chartering Manual consistent with congressional objectives.[22]

When appropriate, the Board has also adopted regulations designed to guard against excessive expansions.[23]

The April 8, 2026, proposed rule was designed to address an unintended consequence stemming from the fraternal association example of an incidental client-customer relationship. As discussed in the preambles to the proposed rule and this final rule, the fraternal association example had led to the conclusion that, if a group required its members to buy a good, product, or service from the organization as a condition of membership, the group was automatically disqualified. This final rule clarifies that this example no longer automatically disqualifies such groups as associations that are based primarily on a client-customer relationship. The Board expects this change to enhance access to reliable financial services, especially for those of modest means, while reducing confusion. As discussed in this preamble, the Board notes that this change is distinct from the long-standing policy that associations that are based primarily on a client-customer relationship do not meet associational common bond requirements.

Excluding associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship will continue to serve as an effective gatekeeper to prevent unqualified groups from chartering or joining FCUs. The Board further notes that other provisions, like the threshold purpose requirement and the totality of the circumstances test, are designed to identify unqualified groups.[24]

Lastly, NCUA has additional safeguards to protect the integrity of field of membership requirements, such as conducting quality assurance reviews and investigating field of membership complaints.[25]

Accordingly, the Board disagrees with the comment that the proposal could result in eroding statutory field of membership restrictions contrary to congressional intent. Thus, the Board has made no changes in response to this comment.

Comments on Defining a Client-Customer Relationship

Several commenters requested clearer guidance on defining a client-customer relationship, particularly the meaning of “primarily” and “incidental.” One commenter recommended defining a client-customer relationship as one in which the organization's sole purpose is selling a good, product, or service to its clients or customers. This commenter suggested a definition focusing on whether a qualifying association would still exist without the client-customer relationship, or whether the common bond is contingent upon the transaction.

AGENCY:

Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.

ACTION:

Final rule.

SUMMARY:

The Board is amending Regulation D, Reserve Requirements of Depository Institutions, to reflect the annual indexing of the reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche for 2027. The annual indexation of these amounts is required notwithstanding the Board's action in March 2020 of setting all reserve requirement ratios to zero. The reserve requirement exemption amount for 2027 will remain $39.2 million, unchanged from 2026, consistent with the Federal Reserve Act (the “Act”). The Board is amending Regulation D to set the amount of the low reserve tranche at $688.5 million (increased from $674.1 million in 2026). The adjustment to the low reserve tranche is derived using a statutory formula specified in the Act. The annual indexation of the reserve requirement exemption amount and low reserve tranche is required by statute but will not affect depository institutions' reserve requirements, which will remain zero.

DATES:

Effective date:
December 18, 2026.

Compliance dates:
The new low reserve tranche will apply beginning January 1, 2027.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Benjamin Snodgrass, Special Counsel (202/263-4877), Legal Division; Kristen Payne, Lead Financial Institution and Policy Analyst (202/306-9573), Division of Monetary Affairs; for users of TTY/TRS, please call 711 from any telephone, anywhere in the United States, or (202/263-4869); Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 20th and C Streets NW, Washington, DC 20551.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Section 19(b)(2) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 461(b)(2)) requires each depository institution to maintain reserves against its transaction accounts and nonpersonal time deposits, as prescribed by Board regulations, for the purpose of implementing monetary policy. The Board's actions with respect to this provision are discussed below.

I. Reserve Requirements

Section 19(b) of the Act authorizes different ranges of reserve requirement ratios depending on the amount of transaction account balances at a depository institution. Section 19(b)(11)(A) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 461(b)(11)(A)) provides that a zero percent reserve requirement ratio shall apply at each depository institution to total reservable liabilities that do not exceed a certain amount, known as the reserve requirement exemption amount. Section 19(b)(11)(B) provides that, before December 31 of each year, the Board shall issue a regulation adjusting the reserve requirement exemption amount for the next calendar year if total reservable liabilities held at all depository institutions increase from one year to the next. The Act requires the percentage increase in the reserve requirement exemption amount to be 80 percent of the percentage increase in total reservable liabilities of all depository institutions over the one-year period that ends on the June 30 prior to the adjustment. No adjustment is made to the reserve requirement exemption amount if total reservable liabilities held at all depository institutions should decrease during the applicable time period.

Total reservable liabilities of all depository institutions decreased by 2.4 percent, from $21,103 billion to $20,588 billion, between June 30, 2025, and June 30, 2026.[1]

Accordingly, the reserve requirement exemption amount for 2027 will remain at $39.2 million, unchanged from its level in 2026.[2]

Pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 461(b)(2)), transaction account balances maintained at each depository institution over the reserve requirement exemption amount and up to a certain amount, known as the low reserve tranche, may be subject to a reserve requirement ratio of not more than 3 percent (and which may be zero). Transaction account balances over the low reserve tranche may be subject to a reserve requirement ratio of not more than 14 percent (and which may be zero). Section 19(b)(2) also provides that, before December 31 of each year, the Board shall issue a regulation adjusting the low reserve tranche for the next calendar year. The Act requires the adjustment in the low reserve tranche to be 80 percent of the percentage increase or decrease in total transaction accounts of all depository institutions over the one-year period that ends on the June 30 prior to the adjustment.

Net transaction accounts of all depository institutions increased 2.7 percent, from $17,012 billion to $17,465 billion, between June 30, 2025, and June 30, 2026.[3]

Accordingly, the Board is amending Regulation D to set the low reserve tranche for net transaction accounts for 2027 at $688.5 million, an increase of $14.4 million from 2026.

The new low reserve tranche will be effective for all depository institutions beginning January 1, 2027.

Effective March 26, 2020, the Board reduced reserve requirement ratios on all net transaction accounts to zero percent, eliminating reserve requirements for all depository institutions. The annual indexation of the reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche for 2027 is required by statute but will not affect depository institutions' reserve requirements, which will remain zero.

II. Regulatory Analysis

Administrative Procedure Act

The provisions of 5 U.S.C. 553(b) relating to notice of proposed rulemaking have not been followed in connection with the adoption of these amendments. The amendments involve expected, ministerial adjustments

( printed page 74070)

prescribed by statute and by the Board's policy concerning reporting practices. The adjustments in the reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche serve to reduce regulatory burdens on depository institutions. Accordingly, the Board finds good cause for determining, and so determines, that notice in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 553(b) is unnecessary.

Regulatory Flexibility Act

The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) does not apply to a rulemaking where a general notice of proposed rulemaking is not required.[4]

As noted previously, the Board has determined that it is unnecessary to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking for this final rule. Accordingly, the RFA's requirements relating to an initial and final regulatory flexibility analysis do not apply.

Paperwork Reduction Act

In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,[5]

the Board reviewed this final rule. No collections of information pursuant to the Paperwork Reduction Act are contained in the final rule.

Further classification changes are summarized as follows:

The Postal Service will apply a flat 11 percent fuel surcharge to domestic Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Parcel Select, and USPS Ground Advantage packages. Initially, the fuel surcharge will be static but eventually the Postal Service intends that it will adjust the surcharge on a weekly basis, based on average fuel prices reported by the Energy Information Administration (EIA). The new, permanent surcharge is set to take effect on the expiration date of the current time limited price change that has been in place since April 26, 2026.

The Postal Service will introduce a repricing fee for postage overpayments and underpayments caused by inaccurate dimensions or weight. For an underpayment, the fee will equal 20 percent of the unpaid amount and will be added to the postage due. For an overpayment, 20 percent will be deducted from the refundable amount, subject to Postal Service refund rules.

The Noncompliance Fee will be renamed the Dimension and Weight Noncompliance Fee and will apply only when dimensions or weight are missing.

The proposed changes to Premium Forwarding Service clarify that the online enrollment fee is annual. The Postal Service will also add Priority Mail Express as an option under Premium Forwarding Service Residential (PFSR) and Premium Forwarding Service Commercial (PFSC) and add Priority Mail Flat Rate Envelopes, Priority Mail Sacks, Priority Mail Express Flat Rate Envelopes, and Priority Mail Express Sacks options for PFSC. PFSC customers may control reshipment frequency for periods of up to 12 months.

The Postal Service will introduce a Shipping Label Noncompliance Fee under Domestic Competitive products for incorrect barcode symbology or constructs.

The Postal Service will expand the number of Price Groups for Priority Mail Express International (PMEI) Flat Rate Envelope from 8 to 20 groups and the number of Price Groups for Priority Mail International (PMI) Flat Rate Envelopes and Boxes from 8 to 20 groups.

The Postal Service will add USPS Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) as an optional feature for International Priority Airmail (IPA) to more accurately reflect timing, payment and procedures related to USPS DDP.

The Postal Service will revise the country group assignments for PMEI, PMI, IPA, and First-Class Package International Service (FCPIS) in, and to the format of, Part D Country Price Lists for International Mail so that it can price these products more effectively.

AGENCY:

Bureau of Land Management, Interior.

ACTION:

Notice of Realty Action.

SUMMARY:

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposes to offer 20 parcels of public land, totaling 200.64 acres in the Las Vegas Valley (Valley), by modified competitive sale at no less than each parcel's fair market value (FMV) pursuant to the Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act of 1998 (SNPLMA), as amended. The sale would be processed in conformance with applicable provisions of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) and BLM regulations. A 4.88-acre parcel proposed for inclusion in the sale was previously part of Recreation and Public Purposes (R&PP) Act lease N-75746. At the request of the lessee, the City of Las Vegas, the BLM approved the relinquishment of these acres from the lease. Because the parcel is no longer subject to the R&PP lease, the BLM proposes to modify the R&PP classification by removing the classification from the 4.88-acre portion of the parcel. This modification is necessary because lands that retain R&PP classification are not available for disposal under SNPLMA, and removing the classification makes parcel NVNV106381471 eligible for nomination in the 20-Parcel SNPLMA Land Sale.

DATES:

The BLM will accept written comments regarding the proposed sale and modification to the R&PP classification until January 4, 2027. The BLM will publish this notice of realty action once a week for 3 consecutive weeks in the Las Vegas Review-Journal newspaper. The BLM intends to open the sale for bidding on February 9, 2027, at 8:00 a.m. Pacific Time (PT).

Submit comments to the address in the
ADDRESSES
section. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personally identifiable information in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including any personally identifiable information—may be made publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your personally identifiable information from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Any comments regarding the proposed sale will be reviewed by the BLM Nevada State Director or other authorized official of the Department of the Interior, who may sustain, vacate, or modify this realty action in response to such comments. In the absence of any comments, this realty action will become the final determination of the Department of the Interior.

The use of the modified competitive sale method is consistent with 43 CFR 2711.3-2. Public lands may be offered for sale by modified competitive bidding procedures when the authorized officer determines it is necessary based on public policies. Utilizing an online auction would support Presidential Memorandum,
Delivering Emergency Price Relief for American Families and Defeating the Cost-of-Living Crisis
(January 20, 2025) and encourage greater participation by qualified bidders.

Federal law requires that bidders must be:

(1) A citizen of the United States, 18 years of age or older;

(2) A corporation subject to the laws of any state or of the United States;

(3) A state, State instrumentality, or political subdivision authorized to hold property; or

(4) An entity legally capable of conveying and holding lands or

( printed page 74603)

interests therein under the laws of the State of Nevada.

The successful bidder must submit proof of citizenship or articles of incorporation within 30 days from receipt of acceptance of bid letter. Evidence of United States citizenship is a birth certificate, passport, or naturalization papers. Citizenship documents or Articles of Incorporation (as applicable) must be provided to the BLM LVFO for each sale.

To participate in the BLM bidding process, you must register and obtain a bidder number. Registration for online bidding will be available prior to the sale date at Efficient Markets' website
https://www.efficientmarkets.com.
In the listings section of the website, click on the “Register” button on the “BLM Nevada SNPLMA Land Sale” tile to register for the sale. A free Efficient Markets account is required to register. To review the listings, obtain maps, and get information on how to submit competitive online bids, click on the “View Listings” button on the “BLM Nevada SNPLMA Land Sale” tile in the listings section of the website. A submitted online internet bid is a binding offer to purchase.

To participate in this sale, prospective buyers must create an Efficient Markets account, complete the Efficient Markets Bidding Terms Agreement, request a bidding allowance, and register for the BLM Nevada 20-Parcel SNPLMA Land Sale. Efficient Markets may require approximately five business days to determine bidder's financial qualifications. Additional information on how to register at Efficient Markets may be found at
https://www.efficientmarkets.com.
Assistance creating an Efficient Markets account and registering for the sale is available by telephoning the Efficient Markets' Government Resources department at 877-351-4488 and by using the following link to create a Buyer's Account:
https://www.efficientmarkets.com
and create a Basic Account. After the account is created, complete your profile by submitting bank account information and requesting a bid allowance. The following information will be required:

Bank Name

Banker's Name

Telephone Number of Banker

Address of Bank

Requested Bid Allowance amount.

Efficient Markets will verify the Bank Name is a recognized financial institution and contact the banker to ask if the prospective buyer has the financial means to cover the requested Bid Allowance, which is the limit or ceiling for bids and is NOT recorded as a bid or offer per property at auction. Upon receiving an affirmative answer, the allowance will be granted.

Important notes regarding your Bid Allowance:
For security reasons, a bidder must contact its banker and grant permission to speak to Efficient Markets about its Bid Allowance request. Efficient Markets will not request the account balance or ask any questions about assets or lines of credit. Efficient Markets will not request the bank account number, nor can it withdraw funds.

The auction website is open to the public. The internet-based land sale can be observed in real-time. However, you must register as a bidder on the website in advance to submit bids for a parcel. The auction website will be active and available for use approximately 10 days after the date of this notice and will remain available for viewing until the completion of the auction. The available parcels listed in this notice will be detailed on Efficient Markets website. Interested parties may visit the website at any time. Potential bidders may register for the online auction as soon as the auction website is active.

Potential bidders are encouraged to visit the website prior to the start of the open bidding period to become familiar with the site and review the bidding instructions available at
https://www.efficientmarkets.com.
Supporting documentation is available on the website to familiarize new users to the process and answer frequently asked questions.

Payments to the BLM will not be made through the auction website. At the conclusion of the final parcel's bidding period, the successful bidder for each parcel will be provided instructions by the online auction system via email on how to make the required payment to the BLM. In addition, you may be required to pay a commission fee to Efficient Markets of 1.5 percent of the highest qualifying bid for each parcel purchased by successful bidders. Efficient Markets will submit a separate invoice via email to each successful bidder for the total amount due to the BLM and a separate invoice for the amount due to Efficient Markets.

Parcels will begin online bidding at the established FMV. Each parcel will have its own unique open bidding period, with start and stop times clearly identified on the auction website. The open bidding period for each parcel will run for 24 hours from start to finish, and only bids placed during this 24-hour period will be accepted. Each parcel will close bidding sequentially so that each bidder will know if it is the highest winning bid before subsequent parcels close. The website will display each current high bid, and the high bid bidder's number.

https://www.txse.com/​reuglations/​rules-filings), and at the principal office of the Exchange.

II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change

In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below.

( printed page 74634)

The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.

A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change

1. Purpose

The Exchange proposes to amend Section A (Transaction Fees) and Section F (Lead Market Maker Program) of the TXSE Fee Schedule to: (i) increase the rebate provided for orders that add displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00; (ii) increase the fee for orders that add or remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00; (iii) reduce the fee for orders that add or remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced below $1.00; (iv) introduce an enhanced rebate designed to incentivize displayed liquidity in TXSE-listed corporate securities; and (v) amend certain definitions and add notes to the Lead Market Maker Program. The Exchange proposes to implement these changes effective on November 2, 2026.[3]

The Exchange's Fee Schedule sets forth the standard rebates and fees applied per share for orders that add and remove liquidity, respectively. Currently, TXSE provides a rebate of $0.0031 per share for orders priced at or above $1.00 that add displayed liquidity to the Exchange and charges a fee of $0.0030 per share for orders that remove displayed liquidity from the Exchange.[4]

For securities priced below $1.00, the Exchange provides a rebate of 0.15% of total dollar value (“TDV”) for orders that add displayed liquidity to the Exchange and charges a fee of 0.15% of TDV for orders that remove displayed liquidity from the Exchange.[5]

The Exchange currently charges a fee of $0.0002 per share for orders that add non-displayed liquidity to the Exchange or remove non-displayed liquidity from the Exchange in securities priced at or above $1.00. The Exchange currently charges a fee of 0.05% of TDV for orders that add non-displayed liquidity to the Exchange or remove non-displayed liquidity from the Exchange in securities priced below $1.00.

Base Rates

The Exchange now proposes to amend its base rates applicable to orders that add displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00. The proposed rebate for orders that add displayed liquidity to the Exchange is $0.0032 per share, an increase of $0.0001 from the current rate of $0.0031 per share. In addition, the Exchange proposes to amend its base rates applicable to orders that add or remove non-displayed liquidity in both securities priced at or above $1.00 and securities priced below $1.00. For orders that add or remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00, the Exchange proposes to charge a fee of $0.0006, an increase of $0.0004 from its current rate of $0.0002 per share. For orders that add or remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced below $1.00, the Exchange proposes to make these executions free.

The purpose of revising the rates associated with adding and removing displayed and non-displayed liquidity is for business and competitive reasons, as the proposed change is intended to incentivize Members [6]

to submit displayed liquidity to the Exchange by providing a higher rebate for displayed orders that add liquidity to the Exchange and charging a higher fee for non-displayed orders that add liquidity to the Exchange or remove liquidity from the Exchange in securities priced at or above $1.00. The Exchange notes that its proposed base rebate for orders that add liquidity to the Exchange in securities priced at or above $1.00 would remain significantly higher than the base rebates provided by competitors for orders that add displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00.[7]

The Exchange notes that its proposed fee for orders that add non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00 is similar to at least one competitor.[8]

The Exchange's proposed fee for orders that remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00 would remain lower than the fees assessed by competitors for orders that remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00.[9]

The Exchange's proposal to make executions free in all non-displayed orders that add liquidity to the Exchange in securities priced below $1.00 aligns with the pricing that competitors offer for similar executions.[10]

In addition, the Exchange's proposal to make executions free in all orders that remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced below $1.00 differs from competitors in that many competitors assess a fee for non-displayed orders that remove liquidity.[11]

In totality, the Exchange believes its proposed fee structure is appropriate in furthering its goal of encouraging Members to submit displayed liquidity to the Exchange as it provides a competitive rebate to Members who add displayed liquidity to the Exchange and charges a fee to those Members who either remove displayed liquidity in all securities or who add or remove non-displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00.

Displayed Liquidity Enhanced Rebate

The Exchange next proposes to introduce an enhanced rebate designed to incentivize quoting in TXSE-listed corporate securities. The Exchange proposes to provide an enhanced rebate of $0.0038 per share in securities priced at or above $1.00 to Members that add displayed liquidity in a TXSE-listed corporate security. The enhanced rebate would not apply to securities priced below $1.00.

The proposed enhanced rebate is designed to encourage Members to submit displayed liquidity to the Exchange in TXSE-listed corporate securities, which contributes to a deeper, more liquid market and provides additional execution opportunities for active market participants. By offering enhanced rebate opportunities to incentivize increased liquidity provision, the

( printed page 74635)

Exchange seeks to encourage greater trading activity and additional execution opportunities for Members, thereby promoting more robust price discovery and improving overall market quality for all market participants.

Lead Market Maker Program

The Exchange next proposes edits to certain definitions found within Section F (Lead Market Maker Program) of the Fee Schedule. The Exchange introduced its Lead Market Maker (“LMM”) Program in September 2026.[12]

The Exchange's LMM Program offers daily stipends paid by the Exchange to LMMs that achieve certain Minimum Performance Standards [13]

in TXSE-listed symbols. The Exchange now proposes to amend the definition of “Size Near the Inside” and “Time at NBBO” to more accurately reflect the Exchange's calculation of those criteria. “Size Near the Inside” is currently defined as “. . .the average notional depth within 25 basis points of the NBBO.” [14]

The Exchange proposes to revise the definition of “Size Near the Inside” to state “. . .the minimum notional value of both bids and offers within 0.25% of the NBBO for at least 95% of the trading day.” The Exchange notes that this change will continue to measure notional depth relative to the NBBO, but would require the LMM to have a notional depth within 0.25% of each of the NBB and NBO for 95% of the trading day rather than looking at an average of total depth within 25 basis points of the NBBO. The Exchange notes that each of the Signature, Premier, and Core Tiers on the current Fee Schedule indicates the minimum notional value that must be provided on each side of the NBB and NBO.[15]

The addition of the 95% threshold is intended to align the calculation of “Size Near the Inside” with the calculation of “Layered Depth” [16]

and is generally in-line with similar criteria of competitor exchange LMM programs.[17]

“Time at NBBO” is currently defined as “. . .the percentage of time during Regular Trading Hours [18]

in which the LMM maintains both a bid and offer at the NBBO with at least $10,000 notional at each of the NBB and NBO.” [19]

The Exchange proposes to revise the definition of “Time at NBBO” to state “. . .the average of (a) the percentage of time the LMM has at least $10,000 notional at the NBB and (b) the percentage of time the LMM has at least $10,000 notional at the NBO.” This change is designed to account for situations where an LMM may have a valid business reason for quoting the NBB or NBO with the required notional value at different times throughout a trading day. For instance, an LMM's inventory position and exposure to additional purchases or sales may warrant greater participation at the inside market on one side of the NBB or NBO than the other.[20]

Under the current definition of “Time at the NBBO”, an LMM participating at the NBB or NBO without the required notional value throughout Regular Trading Hours would not satisfy the “Time at NBBO” criteria if it did not have the required depth at the NBB and NBO for the requisite amount of time during Regular Trading Hours. Under the proposed definition, however, the Exchange would use the average of the percentage of time that the LMM quoted at each of the NBB and NBO, which would reward LMMs that have valid business cases for having different notional at the NBB and NBO at different times during Regular Trading Hours.

In addition, the Exchange proposes to introduce a “Notes” section to Section F of the Fee Schedule. Under the proposed “Notes” section, the Exchange proposes to add two notes that provide additional clarity to how it performs certain calculations related to the Minimum Performance Standards. First, the Exchange proposes to add the following note: “Periods during which the SIP NBBO is missing, invalid, locked, or crossed are treated as ineligible and excluded from denominators for NBBO-referenced metrics.” Second, the Exchange proposes to add a note stating: “Certain percentage-based thresholds set forth in the Program shall be adjusted for leveraged ETPs to reflect the product's stated leverage factor. The adjusted threshold shall equal the stated threshold multiplied by the absolute value of the leverage factor (
e.g.,
2 for a 2x product, 3 for a 3x product, irrespective of direction). The percentage adjustment applies to the following standards: the basis point threshold of Maximum LMM Spread; [21]

the basis point threshold of Size Near the Inside; the percentage threshold of Layered Depth; the basis point threshold of Opening/Closing Auction Depth; [22]

the basis point threshold of Opening/Closing Auction Reference Price.[23]

Notional dollar thresholds are not

( printed page 74636)

subject to the leverage adjustment and apply as stated in the applicable tier.” Each of the proposed revisions to the definitions of “Size Near the Inside” and “Time at NBBO” and proposed additions to the proposed “Notes” section is intended to provide additional clarity to LMMs and other market participants regarding how the Minimum Performance Standards are calculated.

2. Statutory Basis

The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act. The Exchange believes that the proposed fee changes are consistent with the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act [24]

in that they are designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest, and, particularly, are not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange also believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with the provisions of Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,[25]

in that it is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Members and other persons using its facilities.

[Release No. 34-106912; File No. SR-OCC-2026-012]

November 16, 2026.

Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act” or “Act”),[1]

and Rule

( printed page 74639)

19b-4 thereunder,[2]

notice is hereby given that on November 4, 2026, The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared primarily by OCC. OCC filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) [3]

of the Act and paragraph (f) or Rule 19b-4 [4]

thereunder, such that the proposed rule change was immediately effective upon filing with the Commission. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.

I. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change

This proposed rule change would implement a fee holiday for the period beginning December 1, 2026, and ending December 31, 2026. Pursuant to OCC's Capital Management Policy, which the Commission has approved as an OCC rule, when OCC's liquid net assets funded by equity (“LNAFBE”) exceed 110% of OCC's Target Capital Requirement and other approved capital needs, OCC may use tools it deems appropriate to lower costs for clearing members including by implementing a fee holiday. OCC has filed proposed changes to its schedule of fees as Exhibit 5 to File Number SR-OCC-2026-012. Material proposed to be added to OCC's schedule of fees as currently in effect is underlined and material proposed to be deleted is marked in strikethrough text. All capitalized terms not defined herein have the same meaning as set forth in the OCC By-Laws and Rules.

II. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change

In its filing with the Commission, OCC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. OCC has prepared summaries, set forth in sections (A), (B), and (C) below, of the most significant aspects of these statements.

(A) Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change

Founded in 1973, OCC operates as a central counterparty (“CCP”) under the jurisdiction of both the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”). As a registered clearing agency under the SEC's jurisdiction, OCC is the sole clearing agency for equity options listed on national securities exchanges. As a registered Subpart C DCO under the CFTC's jurisdiction, OCC clears and settles transactions in futures and options on futures. OCC also provides central counterparty clearing and settlement services for securities lending transactions. In its role as a CCP, OCC guarantees the performance of its Clearing Members for all transactions cleared by OCC by becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. Given OCC's critical role, OCC has been designated by the Financial Stability Oversight Council as a systemically important financial market utility (“SIFMU”) under Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, entitled the Payment, Clearing and Settlement Supervision Act of 2010 (“Clearing Supervision Act”).[5]

Beginning in January 2025, OCC increased its clearing fee to $0.025 per contract in part to cover increased capital expenditures and decreasing interest income. Over the past several years, OCC has incurred significant expenses due to investments in a modernized technology infrastructure tied to the development and future launch of OCC's new clearing system, Ovation. This new system will improve efficiency both for the industry and OCC. This has come with increased costs, however, with expense growth in cloud technology, hardware, software, data centers, and disaster recovery; headcount increases and wage inflation; and increased costs related to regulatory obligations. However, given the high clearing volumes over the first half of 2025, OCC implemented a fee holiday for December 2025 effectively returning excess capital to market participants. Clearing volume during the first half of 2026 has been similarly strong and OCC's LNAFBE exceeds 110% of its Target Capital Requirement and appears likely to remain above that mark for the remainder of 2026 and 2027. OCC is therefore using the tools outlined in its Capital Management Policy and returning capital to market participants by implementing a fee holiday for December 2026.

1. Purpose

Background

As the sole clearing agency for standardized equity options listed on national securities exchanges registered with the Commission, and with respect to OCC's clearance and settlement of futures and stock loan transactions, OCC maintains policies and procedures to manage the risks borne by OCC as a central counterparty. One such risk that OCC manages is general business risk, that is, the risk of potential impairment to OCC's financial position resulting from a decline in revenues or an increase in expenses. To manage this risk and help to ensure that OCC can continue operations and services as a going concern if general business losses materialize, OCC has adopted its Capital Management Policy,[6]

which provides the framework by which OCC manages its capital. Amending OCC's schedule of fees is one action used by OCC to manage its capital.

Pursuant to OCC's rule-filed Capital Management Policy, and as required by Exchange Act rules applicable to OCC,[7]

OCC must maintain LNAFBE [8]

sufficient to cover at least six months of operating expenses, among other measures

( printed page 74640)

(“Target Capital Requirement”). Because OCC is required to maintain such funds, the LNAFBE used to meet the Target Capital Requirement cannot be used to cover operational expenses and any increase in expenses must be covered by current revenue or cash held in excess of the Target Capital Requirement. The Capital Management Plan further sets 110% of the Target Capital Requirement as an early warning threshold. If LNAFBE falls below the early warning threshold, OCC management and Board must discuss whether a fee increase is necessary.

In the filing to implement the 2025 fee increase (“2025 Fee Filing”),[9]

OCC projected that its LNAFBE would fall below OCC's Target Capital Requirement by the end of Q1 2025 and took action prior to hitting the early warning threshold. At the time, OCC stated it did not believe it would be prudent, given its designation as a SIFMU, to allow its LNAFBE to decline past the early warning threshold prior to taking action to ensure that OCC maintains sufficient LNAFBE to satisfy its regulatory requirements and so that it may continue to operate as a going concern if it were to experience general business losses.[10]

However, in the 2025 Fee Filing, OCC emphasized its commitment to aligning its revenues with its costs and capital needs and stated that, consistent with its past practice, if revenues exceed costs and OCC's LNAFBE is above the early warning threshold, OCC would consider utilizing tools to lower the cost of clearing for market participants, as provided under its Capital Management Policy.[11]

Later in 2025, OCC followed through and implemented a fee holiday for December 2025 to help lower clearing costs for market participants.[12]

Today, OCC is continuing this practice and instituting a fee holiday for December 2026.

Proposed Fee Holiday

OCC proposes to implement a fee holiday for the month of December 2026. OCC has in place policies and procedures, including the Capital Management Policy, to control costs and regularly review fees and operating expenses, including during its annual budgeting process. Consistent with the Capital Management Policy, OCC set its clearing fees based on factors including OCC's annual budgeted or forecasted operating expenses and projected revenue. However, clearing volume, and therefore revenue, have outpaced projections and OCC currently has LNAFBE in excess of its early warning threshold. In addition to clearing fees, OCC receives revenue from the interest paid on the cash margin collateral it holds with the Federal Reserve System and elsewhere. In October 2026, OCC began paying Clearing Members interest on their margin cash at a rate based on the interest rate OCC receives from the Federal Reserve, less a cash management fee. For budgeting purposes, OCC assumed it would begin paying interest on margin cash in July 2026. Therefore, OCC had three fewer months of interest expenses than anticipated, further contributing to the amount of LNAFBE OCC has in excess of the early warning threshold. The fee holiday will allow OCC to return excess capital to market participants and clearing members while still maintaining sufficient capital to maintain compliance with the Capital Management Policy and regulatory requirements.

In evaluating its current LNAFBE and projections for 2027, OCC determined that a fee holiday is warranted for December 2026. Based on recent volumes, OCC estimates that the fee holiday for the month of December will lead to approximately $77 million in lost revenue. Despite this, OCC believes it will remain above the 2026 early warning threshold ($355.3 million) as well as its projected early warning threshold for 2027 ($390.8 million). To make this determination, OCC evaluated revenue and LNAFBE under a wide range of volume scenarios including current average daily volume (“ADV”), 60 million ADV, and -4% ADV growth. In all scenarios except the negative growth scenario, OCC remained above its early warning threshold through the end of 2027 even with the fee holiday. OCC, however, does not believe the negative growth scenario is realistic, and it would result in ADV decreasing by 50% to 35.5 million contracts a day by the end of 2027. The scenario was selected to illustrate the level of volume decrease that would cause OCC to drop below its early warning threshold. Nonetheless, under this extreme scenario, OCC remained above its early warning threshold through October 2027, meaning OCC would have time to react if the negative ADV growth scenario becomes more realistic.[13]

To enact the proposed changes, OCC would update its schedule of fees as set out below.

| Current fee schedule
(Clearing fees)
| Proposed fee schedule
(fee Holiday December 2026)

| All Transactions $0.025/contract
| All transactions $0.00/contract.

| Minimum Monthly Clearing Fee $200
| $0.00.

OCC proposes to make the removal of the $.025 fee per contract effective December 1, 2026. The removal of the minimum monthly fee of $200 will be made once OCC receives all necessary regulatory approvals. Effective the first trading day of 2027, clearing fees will revert to the fee schedule in effect before December 1, 2026 and OCC will remove the fee holiday from its schedule of fees.

2. Statutory Basis

OCC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act [14]

and the rules and regulations thereunder.

Compliance With Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Act

In particular, OCC believes that the proposed fee change is consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Act,[15]

which requires that the rules of a clearing agency provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its participants. OCC believes that the proposed fee holiday is reasonable because it is designed to decrease the cost of clearing while maintaining sufficient LNAFBE to cover OCC's operating expenses and address potential business or

( printed page 74641)

operational losses so that OCC can continue to meet its obligations as a SIFMU. The reasonableness of the proposal is supported by oversight, transparency, and OCC's past practice, wherever circumstances allow, to utilize tools to lower the cost of clearing for participants.

First, OCC's funding and operations are subject to oversight by OCC's Board and the Commission. OCC's annual budget, compensation for senior management, and capital initiatives are reviewed and approved by its Board-level CPC. OCC's Board is made up of a broad cross-section of options market participants, including public representatives, Clearing Member representatives from Clearing Members of various sizes, and options exchange representatives. At least a majority of the CPC is composed of independent directors, consistent with Commission Rule 17ad-25(e) [16]

and the judgment of the Board.

OCC is also supervised by the Commission throughout the year. Pursuant to Section 807(a) of the Clearing Supervision Act, the Commission's Division of Examinations conducts annual examinations of OCC to determine, among other things, (1) the nature of the operations of, and the risks borne, by OCC; (2) the financial and operational risks presented by OCC to financial institutions, critical markets, or the broader financial system; and (3) the resources and capabilities of OCC to monitor and control such risks.[17]

In addition, changes to OCC's rules, procedures and operations that could materially affect the nature or level of risk presented by OCC are also subject to review by the Commission, in consultation with the Federal Reserve, under Section 806(e) of the Clearing Supervision Act.[18]

Furthermore, the SEC publishes such proposed changes for public comment.

Second, OCC's commitment to reasonable funding is further supported by the transparency it provides on an ongoing basis regarding its financial performance. Each year, OCC publishes its Annual Report, inclusive of its audited financial statements prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. OCC maintains a dedicated website that consolidates its annual reports in a readily accessible place.[19]

On a quarterly basis, OCC also provides unaudited information concerning its total revenues, average daily contract volume and LNAFBE on its “Schedule of Fees” website to aid Clearing Members in assessing the risk associated with a potential Operational Loss Fee in accordance with OCC's capital replenishment plan under its Capital Management Policy.[20]

Department of Health and Human Services

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services

[CMS-8092-N]

RIN 0938-AV84

AGENCY:

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), HHS.

ACTION:

Notice.

SUMMARY:

This notice announces the inpatient hospital deductible and the hospital and extended care services coinsurance amounts for services furnished in calendar year (CY) 2027 under Medicare's Hospital Insurance Program (Medicare Part A). The Medicare statute specifies the formulae used to determine these amounts. For CY 2027, the inpatient hospital deductible will be $1,776. The daily coinsurance amounts for CY 2027 will be as follows: $444 for the 61st through 90th day of hospitalization in a benefit period; $888 for lifetime reserve days; and $222 for the 21st through 100th day of extended care services in a skilled nursing facility in a benefit period.

DATES:

The deductible and coinsurance amounts announced in this notice are effective on January 1, 2027.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Suzanne Codespote, (410) 786-7737 or Yaminee Thaker (410) 786-7921.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

Section 1813 of the Social Security Act (the Act) provides for an inpatient hospital deductible to be subtracted from the amount payable by Medicare for inpatient hospital services furnished to a beneficiary. It also provides for certain coinsurance amounts to be subtracted from the amounts payable by Medicare for inpatient hospital and extended care services. Section 1813(b)(2) of the Act requires the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary) to determine and publish each year the amount of the inpatient hospital deductible and the hospital and extended care services coinsurance amounts applicable for services furnished in the following calendar year (CY).

II. Computing the Inpatient Hospital Deductible for CY 2027

Section 1813(b) of the Act prescribes the method for computing the amount of the inpatient hospital deductible. The inpatient hospital deductible is an amount equal to the inpatient hospital deductible for the preceding CY, adjusted by the Secretary's best estimate of the payment-weighted average of the applicable percentage increases (as defined in section 1886(b)(3)(B) of the Act) used for updating the payment rates to hospitals for discharges in the fiscal year (FY) that begins on October 1 of the same preceding CY, and adjusted to reflect changes in real casemix. The adjustment to reflect real casemix is determined on the basis of the most recent case-mix data available. The amount determined under this formula is rounded to the nearest multiple of $4 (or, if midway between two multiples of $4, to the next higher multiple of $4).

Under section 1886(b)(3)(B)(i)(XX) of the Act, the percentage increase used to update the payment rates for FY 2027 for hospitals paid under the inpatient prospective payment system (IPPS) is the IPPS operating market basket percentage increase, otherwise known as the IPPS market basket update, reduced by an adjustment based on changes in the economy-wide productivity (productivity adjustment) (see section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act). Under section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii) of the Act, for FY 2027, the applicable percentage increase for hospitals that do not submit quality data as specified by the Secretary is reduced by one quarter of the market basket update. We are estimating that after accounting for those hospitals receiving the lower market basket update in the payment-weighted average update, the calculated deductible will not be affected, since the majority of hospitals submit quality data and receive the full market basket update. Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(ix) of the Act requires that any hospital that is not a meaningful electronic health record (EHR) user (as defined in section 1886(n)(3) of the Act) will have three-quarters of the market basket update reduced by 100 percent for FY 2017 and each subsequent FY. We are estimating that after accounting for these hospitals receiving the lower market basket update, the calculated deductible will not be affected, since the majority of hospitals are meaningful EHR users and are expected to receive the full market basket update.

Under section 1886 of the Act, the percentage increase used to update the payment rates (or target amounts, as applicable) for FY 2027 for hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system is as follows:

The percentage increase for long term care hospitals (LTCH) is the LTCH market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment (see section 1886(m)(3)(A) of the Act). In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments and the site-neutral payment rates (see section 1886(m)(5) and (6) of the Act).

The percentage increase for inpatient rehabilitation facilities (IRF) is the IRF market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment in accordance with section 1886(j)(3)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act. In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments (see section 1886(j)(7) of the Act).

The percentage increase used to update the payment rate for inpatient psychiatric facilities (IPF) is the IPF market basket percentage increase reduced by the productivity adjustment (see section 1886(s)(2)(A)(i) of the Act). In addition, these hospitals may also be impacted by the quality reporting adjustments (see section 1886(s)(4) of the Act).

The percentage increase used to update the target amounts for other types of hospitals that are excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system and that are paid on a reasonable cost basis, subject to a rate-of-increase

( printed page 74583)

ceiling, is the IPPS operating market basket percentage increase, which is described at section 1886(b)(3)(B)(ii)(VIII) of the Act and 42 CFR 413.40(c)(3). These other types of hospitals include cancer hospitals, children's hospitals, extended neoplastic disease care hospitals, and hospitals located outside the 50 States, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.

The IPPS operating market basket percentage increase for FY 2027 is 3.2 percent and the productivity adjustment is 0.9 percentage point, as announced in the final rule that appeared in the
Federal Register
on August 4, 2026 entitled, “Medicare Program; Hospital Inpatient Prospective Payment Systems for Acute Care Hospitals (IPPS) and the Long-Term Care Hospital Prospective Payment System and Policy Changes and Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 Rates; Requirements for Quality Programs; Other Policy Changes; and Adoption of Updated Versions of Certain Health Information Technology Standards” (91 FR 49570). Therefore, the percentage increase for hospitals paid under the inpatient prospective payment system that submit quality data and are meaningful EHR users is 2.3 percent (that is, the FY 2027 IPPS operating market basket update of 3.2 percent less the productivity adjustment of 0.9 percentage point). The average payment percentage increase for hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system is 2.48 percent. This average includes long term care hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, inpatient psychiatric facilities and other hospitals excluded from the inpatient prospective payment system. Weighting these percentages in accordance with payment volume, our best estimate of the payment-weighted average of the increases in the payment rates for FY 2027 is 2.32 percent.

To develop the adjustment to reflect changes in real casemix, we first calculated an average casemix for each hospital that reflects the relative costliness of that hospital's mix of cases compared to those of other hospitals. We then computed the change in average casemix for hospitals paid under the Medicare inpatient prospective payment system in FY 2026 compared to FY 2025. (We excluded from this calculation hospitals whose payments are not based on the inpatient prospective payment system because their payments are based on alternate prospective payment systems or reasonable costs.) We used Medicare bills from prospective payment hospitals that we received as of July 2026. These bills represent a total of about 5.6 million Medicare discharges for FY 2026 and provide the most recent case-mix-data available at this time. Based on these bills, the change in average casemix in FY 2026 is −0.2 percent. Based on these bills and past experience, we expect the overall FY 2026 casemix change to be −0.1 percent as the year progresses and more FY 2026 data become available.

Section 1813(b) of the Act requires that the inpatient hospital deductible be adjusted only by that portion of the case mix change that is determined to be real. Real casemix is that portion of casemix that is due to changes in the mix of cases and not due to coding optimization. We are assuming that this increase in casemix is real and not a result of coding optimization.

Thus, the estimate of the payment-weighted average of the applicable percentage increases used for updating the payment rates is 2.32 percent, and the real case-mix adjustment factor for the deductible is −0.1 percent. Therefore, using the statutory formula as stated in section 1813(b) of the Act, we calculate the inpatient hospital deductible for services furnished in CY 2027 to be $1,776. This deductible amount is determined by multiplying $1,736 (the inpatient hospital deductible for CY 2026) by the payment-weighted average increase in the payment rates of 1.0232 multiplied by the increase in real casemix of 0.999, which equals $1,774.50 and is rounded to $1,776 (based on rounding to the nearest multiple of 4).

III. Computing the Inpatient Hospital and Extended Care Services Coinsurance Amounts for CY 2027

The coinsurance amounts provided for in section 1813 of the Act are defined as fixed percentages of the inpatient hospital deductible for services furnished in the same CY. The increase in the deductible generates increases in the coinsurance amounts. For inpatient hospital and extended care services furnished in CY 2027, in accordance with the fixed percentages defined in the law, the daily coinsurance for the 61st through 90th day of hospitalization in a benefit period will be $444 (one-fourth of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(1)(A) of the Act); the daily coinsurance for lifetime reserve days will be $888 (one-half of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(1)(B) of the Act); and the daily coinsurance for the 21st through 100th day of extended care services in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in a benefit period will be $222 (one-eighth of the inpatient hospital deductible as stated in section 1813(a)(3) of the Act).

IV. Cost to Medicare Beneficiaries

V. Waiver of Proposed Rulemaking

We ordinarily publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and invite public comment

( printed page 74584)

Section 1871(a)(2) of the Act provides that no rule, requirement, or other statement of policy (other than a national coverage determination) that establishes or changes a substantive legal standard governing the scope of benefits, the payment for services, or the eligibility of individuals, entities, or organizations to furnish or receive services or benefits under Medicare shall take effect unless it is promulgated through notice and comment rulemaking. Unless there is a statutory exception, section 1871(b)(1) of the Act generally requires the Secretary to provide for notice of a proposed rule in the

Section 1871(b)(2)(C) of the Act provides exceptions from the notice and 60-day comment period, under the good cause standard set forth in 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). 14 CFR Parts 13, 47, 49, 61, 63, 65, 187, and 406

[Docket No. FAA-2026-3538; Notice No. 27-01]

RIN 2120-AM16

AGENCY:

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).

ACTION:

Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).

SUMMARY:

FAA proposes to modernize its payment systems to require electronic payments and eliminate the option to pay by paper payment methods such as cash, money orders, and paper checks. This proposal complies with Executive Order 14247 titled “Modernizing Payments To and From America's Bank Account,” which seeks to increase the efficiency of the Federal Government by phasing out paper receipts and mandating electronic payments to and from agencies.

DATES:

Send comments on or before January 4, 2027.

ADDRESSES:

Send comments identified by docket number FAA-2026-3538 using any of the following methods:

Federal eRulemaking Portal:

and follow the online instructions for sending your comments electronically.

Mail:

Hand Delivery or Courier:
Take comments to Docket Operations in Room W58-213 of the West Building 5th Floor at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590 between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.

Fax:
Fax comments to Docket Operations at (202) 493-2251.

Docket:
