www.regulations.gov
at any time. Follow the online instructions for accessing the docket or go to the Docket Operations in Room W58-213 of the West Building 5th Floor at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590 between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Sierra Elam, Office of Rulemaking, ARM-200, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; (202) 267-7627;
sierra.e.elam@faa.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Executive Summary

A. Overview of Proposed Rule

In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14247 titled “Modernizing Payments To and From America's Bank Account”,[1]

FAA proposes to amend its regulations to stop accepting paper payments, such as cash, money orders, and paper checks, and require electronic payments instead. FAA proposes to amend payment provisions located in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) parts 13, 47, 49, 61, 63, 65, 187, and 406. These payment provisions cover aviation and commercial space transportation-related civil penalties, aircraft registration fees, fees for aircraft recording, duplicate airmen and medical certificates, duplicate knowledge test reports, overflight fees, and FAA services performed outside of the United States.

Sections 47.17, 49.15, 61.29, 63.16, 65.16, and 406.9 only list the option to pay fees by paper payment methods. However, §§ 13.15, 13.16, 13.18, and 187.15 allow for both electronic and paper payment options. FAA proposes to amend these sections to require electronic payments and eliminate the use of paper payment methods.

E.O. 14247 directs the Secretary of the Treasury to review and revise procedures for granting limited exceptions where electronic methods are not feasible. Consistent with E.O. 14247, FAA proposes to allow another payment method in circumstances where another method is otherwise authorized by law.

FAA also proposes to revise the following guidance documents to remove references to paper payment methods: Advisory Circular (AC) Form 8050-1B; AC Form 8050-5; and AC Form 8060-56. FAA will post the drafts of these guidance document revisions to this NPRM's docket for public comment.

B. Statement of the Problem

FAA currently processes paper and electronic payment methods, where applicable. Section 3(c) of E.O. 14247 requires all payments made to agencies to be processed electronically, eliminating the need for processing paper payments by phasing out paper disbursements and receipts. Title 14 of the CFR does not mention paper disbursements issued by FAA, and FAA generally does not issue them. In limited circumstances, however, FAA has issued paper checks, such as for witness fees during litigation, if the witness requests a paper payment. In current practice, FAA requests customers use the United States Treasury Department's website,
Pay.gov,
to pay the fees and penalties listed in §§ 13.15, 13.16, 13.18, 47.17, 49.15, 61.29, 63.16, 65.16, 187.15, and 406.9. Although FAA requests customers use
Pay.gov
for the fees and penalties described in this NPRM, the regulatory text in 14 CFR diverges from this current practice.

( printed page 73706)

As a result, FAA proposes to amend its regulations to accept and process electronic payment methods only for all fees and penalties under 14 CFR. FAA also proposes to revise its guidance documents to direct the use of electronic payment methods rather than paper payment methods. These amendments and revisions would standardize FAA's regulations with current practice and guidance. Consistent with E.O. 14247, this proposal is intended to increase government efficiency and reduce the burdens of processing paper payments for the regulatory community.

C. Summary of the Costs and Benefits

The proposed rule would result in annual cost savings of $99,815 for FAA by eliminating the need to process paper payments. Over five years, these savings sum to $457,125 at three percent discounting, or $409,262 at seven percent discounting, or annualized value of $99,815 (regardless of discounting). The proposed rule would result in $1,425,933 in cost savings in perpetuity.

FAA expects the costs to customers to be de minimis to transition from paper to electronic payments.

II. Authority for This Rulemaking

FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety, including those governing charging and receiving fees for certain services provided by FAA, is found in title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Chapter 1, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority.

This rulemaking is issued under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A—Air Commerce and Safety, Chapter 441—Registration and Recordation of Aircraft, Sections 44101—44106, Section 44107, Recordation of conveyances, leases, and security instruments, Chapter 445—Facilities, Personnel, and Research, Section 44506, Air traffic controllers, Chapter 447—Safety Regulation, Section 44702, Issuance of certificates, Section 44703, Airman Certificates, Section 44728, Flight attendant certification, Section 44748, Aircraft dispatching, Chapter 453—Fees, and Chapter 463—Penalties, Section 46301, Civil penalties. Under those statutory provisions, FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to promote safety in civil air commerce, issuing certificates, charging and receiving fees for such services, and assessing civil penalties. This regulation addresses matters within the scope of that authority.

The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50924 (the Act), authorizes the Secretary of Transportation (Secretary) to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the U.S. or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. Section 50917 provides the Secretary with civil penalty authority for violations falling under Section 50917(a). As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the Administrator to carry out these functions.

III. Background

A. History of Payments to FAA

FAA has collected payments for a variety of services since its inception. Historically, these payments have been made by paper methods to FAA. In 1997, FAA began accepting payments electronically for air traffic services for certain flights operating through the National Airspace System (NAS),[2]

by amending § 187.15(d). Since 1997, FAA's regulations have only been amended twice to accept electronic payments. In 2007, FAA amended § 187.15(a) to allow the use of credit card to pay fees for certification services performed outside the United States.[3]

This action standardized the authorized payment methods for services in part 187. In 2021, FAA amended §§ 13.15(c), 13.16(l), and 13.18(j) to accept electronic payments for civil penalties.[4]

In current practice, FAA accepts payments for these services and penalties through
Pay.gov. FAA also accepts electronic payments for fees listed in §§ 47.17, 49.15, 61.29, 63.16, 65.16, and 406.9, even though the regulatory language for each section does not mention the ability to pay by electronic methods.

IV. Discussion of the Proposal

This rulemaking proposes to conform FAA's regulations to the directive in E.O. 14247 to phase out paper check disbursements and receipts. FAA regulations do not include paper check disbursements, so this rule updates regulations related to paper receipts. The proposed amendments described in this section would require payments made to FAA to be collected and processed electronically [5]

and eliminate the use of paper payment methods unless an exception applies as specified in section 4 of E.O. 14247. This section of the NPRM also describes the proposed revisions to guidance documents associated with the proposed regulatory amendments.

A. Proposed Amendments to Investigative and Enforcement Procedures in Part 13

Part 13 contains procedures for compromising some civil penalties before referring them to the United States Attorney General for prosecution, as well as for assessing other civil penalties administratively, depending on the amount of the civil penalty. FAA currently collects payments for these civil penalties through electronic and paper payment methods. The methods for paying civil penalties are located in §§ 13.15(c)(2)(i), 13.16(l)(1)(i) and (ii), and 13.18(j)(1)(i) and (ii). FAA proposes to streamline these conditions by requiring electronic payments and eliminating the option to pay by paper methods, unless another payment method is otherwise authorized by law.

1. Proposed § 13.15, Civil Penalties Other Than by Administrative Assessment

Civil penalties under § 13.15 pertain to those FAA may settle before referring them to the United States Attorney General for prosecution. These civil penalties are in an amount that exceeds FAA's statutory authority to assess (see 49 U.S.C. 46301(d)(4)). Section 13.15(c)(2)(i) states that persons cited with an alleged violation may respond to a proposed civil penalty by submitting an electronic payment, certified check, or money order. The person who paid the civil penalty will then be sent a letter from an FAA

( printed page 73707)

attorney stating the payment settles the action the person was cited with.

FAA proposes to amend § 13.15(c)(2)(i) to remove the option to pay by certified check or money order. Proposed paragraph (2)(i) would require persons to pay civil penalties under this section by electronic payment unless another payment method is otherwise authorized by law.

2. Proposed § 13.16, Civil Penalties Against Miscellaneous Persons and All Persons for Hazardous Materials Violations

Section 13.16 pertains to civil penalties for all violations, including hazardous materials violations, assessed to persons other than individuals acting as a pilot, flight engineer, mechanic, or repairman. Section 13.16(l)(1)(i) and (ii) describe the options for how to pay these civil penalties. Paragraph (l)(1)(i) lists the option to pay penalties by paper payment and paragraph (l)(1)(ii) lists the option to pay by electronic payment. Both paragraphs direct persons paying a civil penalty under § 13.16 to follow the directions listed in the notice of proposed civil penalty, final notice of proposed civil penalty, or the order assessing civil penalty.

FAA proposes to remove paragraphs (l)(1)(i) and (ii) from § 13.16 and revise paragraph (l)(1) to require electronic payments when a person pays a civil penalty unless another payment method is otherwise authorized by law. This proposed change would eliminate the option to pay civil penalties under § 13.16 by paper payment. FAA also proposes to add “compromise order” to the regulatory text in proposed § 13.16(l)(1) because compromise orders are another type of document that involve a civil penalty payment under § 13.16. In addition, the proposed § 13.16(l)(1) text would replace the word “in” with “for” when referencing the directions specified for the notice of proposed civil penalty, final notice of proposed civil penalty, order assessing civil penalty, or compromise order. Civil penalty payment instructions are not necessarily in these documents and might be provided separately by FAA.

The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3 and EC635T2+ helicopters. Background

EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2020-0102, dated May 6, 2020 (EASA AD 2020-0102) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition on certain AHD Model EC135 P1, EC135 P2, EC135 P2+, EC135 P3, EC135 T1, EC135 T2, EC135 T2+, EC135 T3, EC635 P2+, EC635 P3, EC635 T1, EC635 T2+ and EC635 T3 helicopters. The MCAI states that the master service manual (MSM) for Model EC135 and EC635 does not provide complete instructions for the inspections after a hard landing. This condition, if not corrected, could lead to missed identification of tail rotor control damage, which could result in component or system failure and reduced control of the helicopter.

The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2020-0102, which specifies procedures for inspecting the tail rotor control system and, if a discrepancy is found, accomplishing the applicable corrective actions. The FAA also reviewed Aircraft Maintenance Manual 05-51-00, 6-3, Conditional Inspections after Special Operational Incidents—Inspection,

The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.

Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM

This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2020-0102, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. See “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this proposed AD.

Differences Between This Proposed AD and the MCAI

The MCAI applies to AHD Model EC635 P2+, EC635 P3, EC635 T1, and EC635 T3 helicopters, whereas this proposed AD would not because these model helicopters do not have an FAA type certificate. The MCAI requires accomplishing corrective actions in accordance with the qualified instructions as defined in the MCAI, whereas this proposed AD would require those corrective actions be accomplished in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; or EASA; or AHD Design Organization Approval (DOA).

Additionally, the MCAI requires for certain helicopters, inspecting the helicopter after each hard landing, whereas this proposed AD would require all applicable helicopters to perform these inspections within 12 months after the effective date of this proposed AD. Furthermore, the MCAI specifies that revising the AMP by incorporating the qualified instructions as defined in the MCAI is a terminating action for recording compliance, whereas this proposed AD would require revising the existing aircraft MM or ICA and the existing approved maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, by incorporating certain qualified instructions.

SUMMARY:

The National Park Service (NPS) amends the special regulations for Mammoth Cave National Park to allow bicycle use on approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails throughout the park. This rule also will allow visitors to ride horses on the 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road.

DATES:

This rule is effective December 21, 2026.

ADDRESSES:

Comments received on the proposed rule are available on
https://www.regulations.gov
in Docket No. NPS-2026-0001. A copy of the Mammoth Cave National Park Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment and the associated Finding of No Significant Impact are available online at
https://parkplanning.nps.gov/​maca
by clicking the link entitled “Develop Land and River Trail Management Plan for Mammoth Cave National Park” and then clicking the link entitled “Document List.”

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Barclay Trimble, Superintendent, Mammoth Cave National Park; (202) 758-2180;
Barclay_Trimble@nps.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Background

History, Establishment and Purpose of the Park

Mammoth Cave National Park comprises more than 52,000 acres of land within Edmonson, Hart, and Barren Counties in Kentucky. Within Mammoth Cave National Park is Mammoth Cave. Named for the enormity of its subterranean vaults and the unparalleled extent of its passages, Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world with over 400 miles surveyed to date. The geologic features within the extensive cave system are the product of a unique set of conditions found nowhere else, all of which contribute to the largest, most complex, and best-known karst area in the world. Karst is a geologic term that refers to areas of irregular limestone in which erosion has produced features such as fissures, sinkholes, underground streams, sinking springs, and caverns. The land above the underground formations is characterized by rugged hills, valleys, and forests.

Congress authorized the establishment of the park in 1926, which was officially established in 1941 and added to in 1961 with the acquisition of Great Onyx Cave and Crystal Cave. The legislative history of the establishment of the park recognized the need to protect and conserve the stunning and unique underground formations of the cave system, but also opportunities for recreation that could be provided by lands above ground. The park's enabling legislation directs the NPS to administer the park in accordance with the laws generally applicable to the National Park System, including the NPS Organic Act. That act requires the NPS to promote and

( printed page 74477)

regulate the scenery, natural and historic objects, and wild life in parks and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means that will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations. 54 U.S.C. 100101.

In 2014, the NPS published the foundation document for the park. The document states that the park's purpose is to preserve, protect, interpret, and study the internationally recognized biological and geologic features and processes associated with the longest known cave system in the world, the park's diverse forested, karst landscape, the Green and Nolin rivers, and extensive evidence of human history; and to provide and promote public enjoyment, recreation, and understanding. Today, visitors are drawn to the park by its caves, scenic river valleys, bluffs, forests, and abundant wildlife. Above ground, the park offers opportunities for ranger-led tours, surface walks, camping, hiking, horseback riding, bicycling, scenic drives, canoeing and kayaking, fishing, accessible trails, and picnicking.

Trail Use in the Park

Bicycling is allowed on approximately 19 of the 85 miles of land-based trails within the park. These multi-use trails are the Connector Trail from the Big Hollow Trailhead to the Maple Springs Trailhead (Maple Springs Connector Trail), the Big Hollow Trail, the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail, and the White Oak Trail. Bicycles also are allowed on roads that are open to public motor vehicle traffic and on four administrative roads that are closed to motor vehicle use by the public but open to motor vehicle use by the NPS for administrative purposes (the Crystal Cave, Great Onyx, Three Springs, and Union City administrative roads).

Trails, public roads, and administrative roads that are open to traditional bicycles also are open to two-wheeled electric bicycles (e-bikes). Trail-use of three-wheeled e-bikes is limited to the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail and the Maple Springs Connector Trail. The use of traditional bicycles and e-bikes is governed by State law and NPS regulations that address topics such as speed limits, operation during periods of low visibility, obeying traffic control devices, and unsafe operation. See 36 CFR 4.30.

In addition to opportunities for hiking and bicycling, visitors can ride horses on 54 miles of trail within the park, featuring wooded backcountry routes suitable for different skill levels and ages. The trails include wide, smooth dirt paths that accommodate two riders as well as narrower, single-file ridgeline trails. Horseback riding is prohibited on all park roads pursuant to NPS general regulations that prohibit the use of horses on park roads except in limited circumstances. See 36 CFR 2.16.

Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment

In 2022, the NPS began developing a new land and river trails management plan for the park. The NPS initiated this planning process because previous plans had become outdated, and the condition of the park's trail system had deteriorated in a way that was adversely impacting park resources and the experience of trail users. The new plan would guide trail management for several decades with the purpose of improving access to high-quality land and river-based recreational opportunities for a diverse group of trail users, including hikers, equestrians, mountain bikers, and paddlers.

After the conclusion of a preliminary planning phase that sought feedback from trail users, community groups, and the general public, the NPS published the “Mammoth Cave National Park Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment” (EA) in 2024. The EA analyzed the potential environmental impacts of a no-action alternative that would have continued current management of the trail system and an action alternative that was identified as the NPS's preferred alternative. Under the action alternative, the NPS would add approximately 66 miles of land-based trails to the park trail system. This 72 percent increase in trail mileage would create new opportunities for hiking, horseback riding, and bicycling.

Specific to bicycle use, under the preferred alternative, the NPS would (1) discontinue bicycle use on the White Oak Trail; (2) close and restore to natural conditions the Maple Springs Connector Trail; and (3) construct eight new multi-use trails where bicycle use would be allowed, resulting in a total of approximately 37 miles of trail open to bicycle use.

As described in the EA, trail construction activities would use sustainable trail techniques to manage water and limit erosion, such as trail hardening, grade reversals, outslopes, and other earthwork strategies that improve drainage. These measures would minimize trail widening and trail braiding on new and rehabilitated trails, resulting in less vegetation trampling. The NPS would implement mitigation measures to minimize the impact on native vegetation during construction.

In addition to evaluating the potential impacts of trail construction and modification activities, the EA evaluated the potential impacts of allowing bicycles on the new trails. The EA and an associated written determination required by NPS regulations evaluate the suitability of trail surfaces and soil conditions for accommodating bicycle use, life cycle maintenance costs, safety considerations, methods to prevent or minimize user conflict, and methods to protect natural and cultural resources and mitigate impacts from bicycle use. Under the preferred alternative, the NPS would convert a one-mile section of the Ugly Creek Road from a public road to an administrative road that is closed to motor vehicle use other than vehicles used by the NPS for administrative purposes. Hiking and bicycling would be allowed on the converted section of this road.

The preferred alternative also would open the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road (5.4 miles) to horseback riding. This change would improve the experience of equestrians by providing multiple opportunities for shorter loop rides, and a new opportunity to ride to the river and back from the northern boundary of the park. The NPS does not anticipate there will be conflicts between vehicles, equestrian users, hikers, and bicyclists because the road is used rarely by motor vehicles. All other public and administrative roads would continue to remain closed to equestrian use.

The NPS accepted public comments on the EA for 30 days. In December 2024, following a recommendation by the park superintendent, the Regional Director for Interior Region 2, South Atlantic—Gulf, signed a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) that identified the preferred alternative in the EA as the selected alternative. As stated in the FONSI, the NPS believes the selected alternative will improve the conditions and sustainability of the aboveground land and water trail networks in the park and enhance the diversity and quality of visitor experiences while protecting natural and cultural resources. Implementation of the selected alternative will expand opportunities for visitors to enjoy and recreate within the park.

Final Rule

This rule implements part of the selected alternative in the FONSI by amending the special regulations for the park in 36 CFR 7.36. This rule authorizes the superintendent to

( printed page 74478)

designate approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails for bicycle use in the park. The rule identifies 12 distinct trails that could be designated for bicycle use. Two trails currently designated for bicycle use—the Maple Springs Connector Trail and the White Oak Trail—are removed, consistent with plans to close those trails to bicycle use under the selected alternative. Another currently designated trail—the Mammoth Cave Railroad Bike & Hike Trail—remains on the list and another—the Big Hollow Trail—is listed as three separate segments as identified on park maps.

The rule adds the following eight new trails that will be constructed under the selected alternative:

Brooks Knob Road Cemetery Trail;

Brooks Knob Road Trail (up to gate);

Crystal Cave Road Trail;

East Entrance Trail;

Little Hope Cemetery Trail;

Sugar Sink Connector Trail;

Sugar Sink Trail; and

West Entrance Trail.

The rule includes the approximate mileage of all the identified trails. The rule requires the superintendent to notify the public of designated trails through one or more of the methods identified in 36 CFR 1.7, including publication in the Superintendent's Compendium (or written compilation) of discretionary actions and on maps available at the visitor center and on the park website. NPS regulations at 36 CFR 4.30(i) authorize superintendents to allow electric bicycles on park roads, parking areas, and administrative roads and trails that are otherwise open to traditional bicycles. Accordingly, the superintendent may decide to allow electric bicycles on any of the trails identified in the rule that are open to traditional bicycles and will notify the public pursuant to 36 CFR 1.7.

NPS general regulations in 36 CFR 2.16(c) prohibit the use of horses or pack animals on a park road, except where such travel is necessary to cross to or from designated trails, areas, or privately owned property when no alternative trails or routes have been designated, and when the road is closed to motor vehicles. Neither of these exceptions to the general rule apply to riding horses on the Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road, which is called for in the selected alternative. Special regulations for the park, however, can amend, modify, relax, or make more stringent general regulations in 36 CFR parts 1 through 5 and part 12. See 36 CFR 1.2(c). Accordingly, this rule adds a new paragraph (d) to the special regulations for the park that allows equestrian use on the approximately 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road.

Compliance With NPS Bicycle Regulations

The EA constitutes the planning document and evaluates the criteria required by the NPS's general bicycle regulations at 36 CFR 4.30. Under the selected action in the FONSI, the NPS will allow bicycle use on approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails in the park. The EA evaluates the suitability of each trail surface and soil conditions for accommodating bicycle use, and life cycle maintenance costs, safety considerations, methods to prevent or minimize user conflict, and methods to protect natural and cultural resources and mitigate impacts associated with bicycle use.

The final trail alignments shown on the maps in the EA are based on field surveys and geographic information system (GIS) analysis. The new trail alignments have been determined at the corridor level, defined as a 60-foot-wide corridor within which the new trail would be constructed. Final trail alignments will be determined on the ground upon implementation and in consultation with park natural and cultural resources specialists, which could result in minor adjustments to the trail locations shown on the maps. If a need existed to align a trail outside of the identified corridor, the amended alignment would undergo additional review to avoid or minimize impacts on sensitive resources, and the change would be documented as an amendment to the trails management plan.
